sections.title: The definite article: ο, η, το

body.p: There is no vocative article: **Γιάννη!** "Giannis!", **Κυρία Παπαδάκη!** "Mrs Papadaki!"
Three things make the table easy:

list: Neuter **το/τα** never change between nominative and accusative.
The genitive plural is **των** for all genders.
Masculine and feminine plural nominative are both **οι**.

ex.en: I drink my coffee black (no sugar).

body.tip: **τους** is both the masculine accusative plural article (**τους φίλους** "the friends") and the weak pronoun "them / their" (**τους βλέπω** "I see them", **το σπίτι τους** "their house"). The position tells you which: the article comes before a noun.

solved.q: Give the article: Βλέπω ___ ήλιο (accusative singular, masculine)
Give the article: Το χρώμα ___ θάλασσας (genitive singular)
Give the article: ___ παιδιά παίζουν (nominative plural, neuter)

check.why: καφές is masculine; nominative singular article ο.
Object of θέλω: accusative masculine τον.
κλειδί is neuter: το (nominative and accusative are the same).

sections.title: The indefinite article: ένας, μία, ένα

body.p: It has no plural: **ένα βιβλίο** "a book" but **βιβλία** "books", or **μερικά βιβλία** "some books". It is also the number "one".
Greek uses the indefinite article less than English. Leave it out:

list: after **είμαι / γίνομαι** with jobs and nationalities: **Είναι γιατρός** "She's a doctor", **Είμαι Αμερικανός** "I'm an American";
after **έχω** / **ψάχνω** when the number does not matter: **Έχεις αυτοκίνητο;** "Do you have a car?", **Ψάχνω δουλειά** "I'm looking for a job";
in exclamations with **τι**: **Τι ωραία μέρα!** "What a lovely day!"

ex.el: Ένας φίλος μου μένει στην Κρήτη.
ex.en: A friend of mine lives in Crete.

body.tip: **Μία** and **μια** are the same word. Use **μία** when you mean the number "one" and **μια** for "a": **Θέλω μία, όχι δύο** "I want one, not two"; **μια φορά** "once".

solved.why: No article with jobs after είμαι.

solved.q: Give the indefinite article: Θέλω ___ καφέ.
solved.why: καφές is masculine; accusative έναν (ένα is also heard before consonants).
Exclamations with τι take no indefinite article.

check.why: No article with a job after είμαι.

check.q: "Do you have a car?" (do you own one at all?)
check.why: After έχω in questions about having something at all, no article.
Exclamations with τι take no article.
No article with ψάχνω when any job will do.
No article with jobs after είναι.

body.p: The preposition **σε** "to, in, at, on" joins the definite article into one word. It never stands before a definite article on its own.

ex.en: We're on our way (on the road).
The key is on the table.
The kids are on the swings.

body.p: Before a word without an article, **σε** stays: **σε μια ώρα** "in an hour", **σε ένα λεπτό** "in a minute", **σε εμένα** "to me". Before a vowel it may become **σ'**: **σ' ένα λεπτό**.

body.tip: στη(ν) follows the final -ν rule: **στην Ελλάδα, στην Κρήτη, στην Πάτρα** but **στη Θεσσαλονίκη, στη Ρόδο, στη δουλειά**.

solved.why: σε + την = στην; keep ν before π.

check.why: κουζίνα is feminine; keep ν before κ: στην κουζίνα.
"in a bank": σε μια τράπεζα; with no definite article σε stays.
ο Πειραιάς is masculine: στον Πειραιά.
No definite article, so σε stays a separate word.

sections.title: Where Greek uses the article and English does not

body.p: Greek puts the definite article before:

list: **names of people**: **Ο Γιώργος** ήρθε. "Giorgos came." **Μίλησα με τη Μαρία.** "I spoke to Maria." (but not when you address them: **Γιώργο, έλα!**)
**countries, cities, islands**: **η Ελλάδα**, **η Αθήνα**, **η Κρήτη**, **η Γερμανία**
**abstract and general nouns**: **Η ζωή είναι ωραία.** "Life is beautiful." **Μου αρέσει η μουσική.** "I like music." **Το γάλα κάνει καλό.** "Milk is good for you."
**possessives**: **το σπίτι μου** "my house", **η μητέρα του** "his mother"
**days, months with prepositions**: **την Κυριακή** "on Sunday", **τον Αύγουστο** "in August"
**languages after μιλάω** usually without: **Μιλάω ελληνικά** "I speak Greek", but **Τα ελληνικά είναι δύσκολα** "Greek is difficult" (as a subject).

ex.el: Η Άννα είναι από την Ιταλία.

ex.en: On Sunday we're going to the seaside.

body.p: Leave the article out after **σαν** "like", in many set phrases (**με τα πόδια** keeps it, but **με αυτοκίνητο** "by car"), and after **είμαι** with jobs: **Ο Κώστας είναι μάγειρας.**

body.tip: **Μου αρέσει καφές** is wrong. With **αρέσει** the thing you like is the subject and takes the article: **Μου αρέσει ο καφές**, **Μου αρέσουν τα γλυκά**.

solved.a: Η Μαρία είναι από την Ελλάδα.
solved.why: Article with the name and with the country.
The thing liked is the subject and takes the article.
Days take the accusative article: on Friday = την Παρασκευή.

check.why: Names take the article as subjects: ο Νίκος.
With αρέσει the thing liked is the subject, with its article.
Abstract nouns used generally take the article.
No article when you call someone (vocative).

check.q: "In August we go to the island."
check.why: Time expressions: accusative with article, no preposition.
Means of transport: με + noun without article.
Islands take the article; keep ν before κ.
Article with the name, none with the job.
Accusative article; drop ν before δ.

body.p: Put **το** before almost anything and it becomes a noun: a verb clause, an adverb, a quotation, a letter. This is common in speech and the press.

ex.el: Το να μαγειρεύεις κάθε μέρα είναι κουραστικό.
Το ότι δεν ήρθε με ενόχλησε.
ex.en: The fact that he didn't come annoyed me.

ex.el: Το αύριο δεν το ξέρει κανείς.
ex.en: No one knows what tomorrow brings.
Too much talk is poverty. (proverb: talk less)

body.p: An adjective with the article stands for people or things: **οι νέοι** "young people", **ο μικρός** "the little one / the kid", **η μεγάλη** "the elder (daughter)", **τα καλά** "the good things".

solved.q: Make a noun of the clause: "Waking up early is hard." (ξυπνάω νωρίς)
solved.a: Το να ξυπνάς νωρίς είναι δύσκολο.
solved.why: το να + verb works like an English -ing subject.

solved.q: Translate: "The fact that you called made me happy." (χαίρομαι)
solved.a: Το ότι πήρες τηλέφωνο με χαροποίησε. | Χάρηκα που πήρες τηλέφωνο.
solved.why: το ότι turns a clause into a subject; everyday speech often prefers χάρηκα που...
Adjective with the article = people of that kind.

check.why: το να + verb works as a noun, always neuter singular.
οι παλιοί = old-timers, people of the past.

options: Το αύριο είναι μια άλλη μέρα.
Ο αύριο είναι μια άλλη μέρα.
Η αύριο είναι μια άλλη μέρα.
Αύριο το είναι μια άλλη μέρα.
check.answer: Το αύριο είναι μια άλλη μέρα.
check.why: An adverb made into a noun takes neuter το.
Adjective + article: ο μικρός = the little boy, η μικρή = the little girl.

check.q: Translate: "The fact that he's late doesn't surprise me." (αργεί, μου κάνει εντύπωση)
check.answer: Το ότι αργεί δε μου κάνει εντύπωση.
accept: Το ότι αργεί δεν μου κάνει εντύπωση.
check.why: το ότι + clause as the subject.

check.answer: Το να μαθαίνεις ελληνικά είναι διασκεδαστικό.
check.why: το να + second person singular: the general "you".

title: The article
part: Μέρος Β΄ | Άρθρο και ουσιαστικό | The article and the noun
blurb: The definite and indefinite article in every case, the contractions στο/στη/στον, and where Greek uses an article when English does not.

intro.p: The article is the most useful word in Greek: it tells you the **gender**, **number** and **case** of the noun after it, even when you do not know the noun. If you hear **της**, you know a feminine genitive is coming; if you hear **τους**, a masculine accusative plural (or a genitive plural).

Greek uses the definite article much more than English: with names (**ο Νίκος**), with abstract nouns (**η αγάπη**), with countries and cities (**η Ελλάδα**, **η Αθήνα**) and with possessives (**το σπίτι μου**).
